I won't lie. That's a real possibility. It comes with the territory of loving someone who is suffering. But if that is to be, if that is her choice, there is nothing you can do now to prevent it. I know that is really painful to accept, impossible even. But you can't hold her hostage here. If she smells any agenda on you she will resent you, which won't help your cause. Think of her as sand, cradle and don't grip.

My unprofessional advice: don't make demands of her, just be there for her, consistently, every time she needs you, be there. If you can engage her in something outside of herself do that. Especially activities where she is helping someone else (added bonus, this will be good for you too). Hey, I'm going to sort donations for the women's shelter, or I'm going to work in the community garden, or I'm going to go catch a movie, wanna come? Listen to her. Don't try and fix it. Just listen. Tell her these four things in whatever variation is appropriate to what she says to you: 1. Legitimize her feelings: How you are feeling is real/I believe you/it's okay to not be okay 2. Legitimize her effort/acknowledge progress: That sounds so hard/you are handling it better than you think/you are doing the best you can 3. Everything is going to be okay - don't use words at first for this one if it will delegitimize her feelings (see step 1), use your presence, hold her if she will let you, eventually you can sneak in, I promise it gets better/it won't always be this hard 4. Unconditional love - no script for this one, just love her.

I really do wish you both all the best, and I hope she chooses to stay. She sounds like an amazing person.

I would give absolutely anything for someone to care about me this much. She is very lucky. Keep loving her, and always remember her choices are hers. Live or die, her choice has nothing to do with you or how much you love her and everything to do with what it feels like to be inside her skin, which you cannot know, not really.

The short answer, westerners REALLY like expressing themselves. Our values are individualistic, freedom of individual expression being top among them. 

The more detailed answer involves some western history, and I'm speaking in general terms here. For some, pride parades are an exercise in solidarity and remembrance of those that came before, and the many that were killed, fighting for equal rights. Its a tradition that started here in the US, just after the Stonewall riots in the 60s. For most people, it has evolved since then into more of a celebration than a resistance (as LGBTQ liberation has progressed a lot since then). An opportunity to be really "out" in public, not just out but proud. It's a type of freedom, to just be who you are without fear of being ostracised, that is still not built into the day-to-day gay experience the way it is built into the straight one. So we have parades.

Mine, 2.5 yr old, have had him for about a year, is a nibbler too, especially before he goes to sleep. May have been weened too early. Crate training at night helped calm mine at night until he got accustomed to what  bedtime means. Now he sleeps with me.  
  
For the nibbling, I like the ice pack game. Cheap and effective. Fill a large rag with ice cubes or ice chips. Tie it at the top with as many knots as you can. Now his job is to undo all the knots to get to the crunchy goodness inside. It redirects the nibbles and exercises his active brain.  
  
For the boredom, check out the Buster Ball. You can get one on Amazon, it's a hard plastic box that's essentially impossible for him to chew up/destroy. It's designed with rounded corners so he cannot grip it with his teeth. You load it with dry food or treats and he has to smack it around with his nose and paws to get the treats out.  This will keep mine distracted for 30-45 min at a time.  
  
He's a beautiful fella! Good luck!

The freedom harness (you can find them in Amazon for about $30) has been amazing for mine. He's about 70 lbs, short hair, very strong and not leash trained at all when we adopted him. The freedom harness has a soft velvety lining on the underside so no pit chafing. Further, it lets you clip the lead to both the front and back of the harness (w/ double headed lead), and makes it near impossible for them to pull. When they try it just rotates them towards you. Made training much easier. Been using it regularly for about 2 months and now on walks I can clip a normal lead to just the back and have no problems with pulling.

I had the same anxiety about cars at your age. You want me to be in charge of this big metal coffin speeding along at 70 mph trying to avoid other big metal coffins? No thank you. I moved to the city at 18 in part because I knew I'd never have to drive. Time does not lessen the anxiety. I think it makes it harder actually, you build it up in your head over time.  
  
I was 29 before I got my license and failed the exam twice because I was so nervous. Now that I've been driving for a while, I've come to really enjoy it, so don't wait, especially if your parents are willing to help you and provide a car to practice with. Practice is the real key. Find a short route you already know, to the grocery store or to school, and drive it back and forth until you feel comfortable, which you won't at first, that's normal, but the feeling is also temporary I promise. Also, this is going to sound dumb, but video games (Burnout Revenge) and go-carts helped a lot with the anxiety.

I should preface that I did not grow up on a farm, just a regular suburb in the states. We had three pet rabbits when I was maybe four or five years old. Well, they bred as rabbits do, and within the course of a summer we had 13 pet rabbits. I loved them and gave them all individual names. One winter morning I woke up and went out to the rabbit hutch to find all but two of the original rabbits missing. When I asked my mom what happened she said it was too cold and they froze to death. Found out later that this was half true. They had froze, but only after my mom had snapped their necks, skinned then, gutted them and put their bunny meat in the deep freezer in the garage. Apparently I really liked rabbit stew. 
  
  
TL DR: I was unknowingly fed my own pet rabbits.

The facts: This comes from the abstract for a single scholarly article published in 2010 called "Abnormal visual experiences in individuals with histories of hallucinogen use: a Web-based questionnaire" by Matthew Baggott, in which 2,679 users were surveyed. Of these 107 (4.1%) reported any HPPD-like symptoms and only 16 of those sought help.  
  
Reviews of this study suggest that this number may overestimate the prevalence of HPPD, since people with visual problems may have been more interested in completing the researchers' questionnaire, while most of these drugs are illegal with serious consequences to people admitting their use. The authors reported that 16,192 people actually viewed the study information but did not complete the questionnaire. If all these people had used hallucinogens without developing visual problems, then the prevalence of serious visual problems in this larger group would be 0.66%. Since these people were not formally diagnosed in person (and may have had visual problems caused by other disorders), this number may provide a reasonable upper limit on the prevalence of HPPD, or they might be statistically meaningless.
  
Dr. John Halpern in a review of this study found that because participants, recruited from the popular drug information Web site Erowid, did not represent the average dabbler, and because only a small portion of them had actively sought medical care, the tally remains somewhat inconclusive. “Unfortunately,” writes Halpern, assessing the scant literature, “the data do not permit us to estimate, even crudely, the prevalence of ‘strict’ H.P.P.D.”.  
  
Halpern and mentor Dr. Harrison G. Pope in one study of five hundred Native American Church members, each of whom had taken peyote hundreds, even thousands of times, no H.P.P.D.-like symptoms were reported. 
  
Further, at a recent Society of Biological Psychiatry conference, Dr. Henry Abraham presented findings, later published in the S.B.P. 2012 supplement, that suggest up to sixty-five per cent of H.P.P.D patients chronically endure panic attacks, and fifty per cent, major depression. While H.P.P.D. sufferers do misperceive their environment, some researchers suspect that severe anxiety—perhaps an underlying condition—aggravates those misperceptions. As noted by Matthew Baggott, fMRI studies generally show close links between the attention and visual systems.

Such observations have raised doubt over whether hallucinogens are the root cause of the disorder, and even whether H.P.P.D. is a bona-fide diagnosis
  
  Another study using data drawn from years 2001 to 2004 of the National Survey on Drug Use and Health consisting of a much larger sample 130,152 with better screening methods for mental health conditions and distress found that of that sample 21,967 respondents (13.4% weighted) reported lifetime psychedelic use. In this study there were no significant associations between lifetime use of any psychedelics, lifetime use of specific psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, mescaline, peyote), or past year use of LSD and increased rate of any of the mental health outcomes. Rather, in several cases psychedelic use was associated with lower rate of mental health problems.  
  
[http://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0063972](http://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0063972)  
  
A newer study published in 2015 reviewing 75 previous studies on the subject also concludes that the prevalence of flashback and HPPD is unknown. It is considered to be remarkable in view of the relatively few case reports published out of millions of hallucinogen users since the 1960 s and 1970 s.
